definition: AI sovereignty is a country's or organization's capacity to control their artificial intelligence (AI) technology.
details: This may cover foundational model algorithms, training data, compute infrastructure, applications, governance policies, and talent pipelines. As both public and private organizations adopt AI technology, the transition has raised issues around compliance, safety, and control beyond traditional technology sovereignty and data sovereignty. Countries are also developing native AI capabilities to address national security concerns and protect technological sovereignty in the public sector. In many regulatory frameworks, in addition to data storage, model performance and decision-making reasoning are also subject to scrutiny. Therefore, building control into the architecture has become essential. Beyond traditional IT infrastructure, the scope includes training AI models, such as foundation models and large language models (LLMs), which requires continuous training and updates, as well as inference which happens in real time across complex IT environments. explainer.lead: AI sovereignty asks who can decide how an AI system is built, run, updated, and governed. It matters because control over data alone may not provide control over model behaviour, computing infrastructure, vendors, or public-sector capabilities.

tiers.eli5: AI sovereignty is like being able to run your own kitchen rather than depending completely on someone else to cook for you. You might make everything yourself, or use outside suppliers while keeping the power to set the rules and inspect the results. The main idea is having meaningful control, not necessarily doing every job alone.
tiers.practitioner: In practice, teams may choose on-premise hardware over public cloud facilities, avoid dependence on a single vendor, and retain governance over data and models. Operational scope includes continuous model training and updates as well as real-time inference across complex IT environments. Treating data storage as sufficient is a pitfall when model performance, decision-making reasoning, compliance, and safety also require scrutiny.
tiers.paperLevel: AI sovereignty is an actor's capacity to control its AI technology across foundational model algorithms, training data, compute infrastructure, applications, governance policies, and talent pipelines. The term has no universal definition: in public-sector settings, a hard form can mean complete technological self-sufficiency, while a soft form can retain regulatory control over foreign vendors. Its scope extends beyond technology and data sovereignty, but the sources provide no single metric for determining when sovereignty has been achieved.

explainer.example: An organization deploys an LLM on its own hardware instead of a public cloud, avoids relying on one vendor, and keeps governance over its training data and models. It also controls continuing updates and real-time inference, while reviewing model performance and decision-making reasoning rather than checking only where data is stored.

explainer.intuition: Using an AI service is not the same as controlling it. AI sovereignty concerns how much practical and regulatory power a country or organization retains over the technology and its dependencies.
howItWorks: Identify which parts of AI require control, from infrastructure and data to algorithms and applications.
Include governance policies and talent pipelines alongside technical assets.
Choose a degree of control, ranging from complete self-sufficiency to regulated use of foreign vendors.
Build control into the architecture for training, updates, and real-time inference.
Scrutinize data storage, model performance, and decision-making reasoning where regulation requires it.
explainer.whyItMatters: As AI adoption grows, questions of compliance, safety, and control extend beyond conventional IT infrastructure and data storage. For governments, sovereignty can support national security and public-sector technological independence; for organizations, it can preserve operational control and reduce vendor dependence.
misconceptions: AI sovereignty does not always mean complete self-sufficiency; softer forms can permit foreign vendors under government control and regulation.
It is broader than data sovereignty because it also concerns models, compute, applications, governance, and talent.
It is not limited to training: continuing updates and real-time inference also fall within its scope.
